aiSummary: Speckled trout, bull redfish, and flounder have all been showing well across Choctawhatchee Bay this past week, with guides reporting quality fish and even a 40-inch, 26-lb bull red on a recent bay trip. Water temps are sitting at 86°F and pushing the bite firmly into early morning hours, so plan to be on the water at first light and work efficiently — the full moon's spring tide will add extra tidal push and current to key structure today. A 29% storm chance develops after 4 PM, so most anglers will want to be off the water well before then given the heat index topping 110°F.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel that concentrates bait on both tides. Pilings hold speckled trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum year-round, with the lee-side pilings serving as the prime ambush zone on incoming tides. Keep in mind this is open, exposed water — it's typically the first spot to become unfishable when wind picks up.
bridge.todaysCall: The WNW wind at 5-10 mph will put a light chop on the open water here — manageable this morning but worth monitoring. The full moon spring tide means stronger-than-average current push through this funnel, which is a genuine advantage: bait will be moving through at first light well ahead of the falling tide that bottoms out around 4:07 PM. Work the lee-side pilings hard during that early moving water with a paddle tail or live shrimp. Plan to wrap up by early afternoon — open water and a 29% storm window after 4 PM make this spot a bad place to linger late in the day.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers protected water with a strong year-round redfish population, plus trout and flounder at the mouth. The oyster bars at the creek mouth are the prime focal point, and tree cover keeps the interior a few degrees cooler than the open bay while providing shelter from wind and weather. The upper creek transitions toward brackish water and can hold bass alongside smaller reds.
alaqua.todaysCall: This is a smart pick for a hot Monday — the tree cover will provide meaningful shade relief when the heat index pushes toward 110°F, and the protected nature of the bayou means the WNW wind won't be much of a factor. Hit the oyster bars at the mouth first thing at first light to capitalize on the full moon tidal push and target trout and reds before the tide drops toward low around 4:07 PM. Slightly stained water today actually favors redfish close to structure, so work topwaters and weedless gold spoons along those oyster edges early. Trout action has been solid bay-wide, so don't neglect the mouth with a suspending twitch bait as the tide begins to fall — flounder should also be staging there.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees less fishing pressure than Alaqua and LaGrange, meaning the fish here tend to be less educated and more willing to bite. The interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing territory for reds in under two feet of water. Pompano occasionally show at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer, and the spot is less protected than LaGrange when weather begins to build.
basin.todaysCall: The lighter pressure here makes Basin Bayou worth the run on a day when fish may be spooky from a week of boat traffic elsewhere. Get on the interior grass flats at first light — the full moon spring tide will have water moving, and 86°F temps mean reds will be most active in those first two hours after sunrise. Slightly stained water gives you a little forgiveness on approach during sight-fishing, but keep casts long and entries quiet in the skinny water. Because Basin Bayou is less protected than LaGrange, keep a close eye on building afternoon clouds and be ready to exit well before the post-4 PM storm window opens.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is consistently one of the top trout producers in the area, with legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold redfish year-round. Deep holes inside the bayou hold black drum and sheepshead, and the location is the most protected water on this side of the bay — making it the go-to refuge when weather threatens.
lagrange.todaysCall: LaGrange is arguably the best all-around call for today given the heat, storm risk, and strong bite report. The full moon spring tide will be pushing good current over those oyster bar edges right around first light through mid-morning — prime time for speckled trout on soft plastics or live shrimp under a popping cork. Slightly stained water and a falling tide leading into the 4:07 PM low means fish will stack up on structure, so work the deep holes inside the bayou for black drum and sheepshead as the afternoon progresses. If storms fire after 4 PM, this is the safest spot on the bay to shelter up and wait it out.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, where tidal flow pushes baitfish up the creek on incoming tides and concentrates redfish and trout in the bends and along grass edges. The creek mouth is a prime flounder zone, and the upper section transitions to brackish water that can hold bass alongside smaller reds. It's the shortest and most protected fishery in the area — the safest option when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: For anglers launching from Shipyard Marina, Four Mile Creek is a low-risk, high-reward option today — it's the most protected spot available and the shortest run when afternoon storms become a concern. The outgoing tide running toward the 4:07 PM low will funnel baitfish back toward the creek mouth, so position near the mouth for flounder and trout during that window — flounder have been showing up on bay trips this past week. Work the bends and grass edges with a paddle tail or shrimp on a jig head early, then transition toward the mouth as the tide falls. Being this close to the ramp means you can comfortably fish through midday and still get off the water well before any post-4 PM weather develops.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide spot and one of the most productive trout flats on the bay, with trout consistently stacking on grass in two to four feet of water during summer mornings. Spanish mackerel make appearances at the mouth on moving tides, and the bayou sees regular pressure but produces reliably. Factor in the longer run time from the 331 Bridge area compared to the other bayous.
hogtown.todaysCall: Hogtown is built for mornings like this one — guides have been hammering trout on the grass flats at first light all week, and the full moon spring tide will have water moving over those two-to-four-foot grass areas right at sunrise. Get there early; with 86°F water and a sky that will cloud up as the day goes on, the bite window on the flats is likely compressed to that first two hours of light. Walk the dog on a topwater or throw a Flats Minnow on a light jig head across the grass edges before switching to a popping cork rig as the sun climbs. Account for the longer run time when planning your exit — you'll want to be headed home well before 4 PM given the storm window and open water between here and the ramp.

rocky.aiNote: Rocky Bayou sits inside Fred Gannon Rocky Bayou State Park near Niceville, offering protected, scenic, and significantly less pressured fishing than the bayous closer to the 331 Bridge. Freshwater influence from Rocky Creek makes flounder fishing excellent, and the glass-calm state park coves are ideal for sight-fishing redfish. Mangrove snapper hold near dock pilings, and anglers should factor in the longer run time as this is the furthest location from Shipyard Marina.
rocky.todaysCall: Rocky Bayou's distance from the marina means fewer boats, and that seclusion pays off on a summer weekday — reds in those state park coves will be far less pressured than fish elsewhere on the bay. The freshwater influence keeps water clarity and temp conditions slightly different here, and with 86°F water bay-wide, the shaded coves inside the park will be a genuine relief for both angler and fish. Target redfish on the sight flats early in the glassy morning calm, then work dock pilings for mangrove snapper as the sun gets high and the flats bite slows. The protected nature of Rocky Bayou makes it a reasonable afternoon option, but the long run back to the marina is a real consideration if storms fire after 4 PM — plan your departure time accordingly.
